vignette:
He is 56, a European man who has spent most of his adult life making a living as a musician. He is married, and when he talks about his life before the trauma, he does so in terms of rhythm and routine: rehearsals in the afternoon, performances in the evening, long drives home with equipment in the back, his wife waiting up for him with the kitchen light on. Music has always given shape to his days and a sense of identity. He describes himself, before everything changed, as sociable, disciplined, and at ease in the world of late nights and strangers.

The assault happens after a performance several years ago. He has stayed behind at a venue, as he often does, talking with people after the set while the room empties out and chairs are stacked. He has a few drinks, not enough that he expects trouble, and he remembers feeling tired, slightly dulled, and eager to get home. A man he has met casually through the local music scene offers to help carry some equipment to a back room and then to a car. What follows is something he still struggles to tell in a straight line. He remembers a door closing, the abrupt change in the other man’s tone, the disbelief that freezes him before fear arrives fully. He recalls the smell of stale beer, the pressure of being pinned, and the strange distance that comes over him, as if he is watching the scene from somewhere near the ceiling. His thoughts narrow to fragments: this cannot be happening, stay quiet, get out alive. Afterwards, he drives home in a state he describes as “not entirely in my own body.” He showers for a long time without feeling clean and says nothing to his wife.

In the weeks that follow, he tries to outrun it by keeping busy. He accepts extra gigs, practices obsessively, and tells himself that naming what happened would make it real in a way he cannot bear. But the memory forces itself in anyway. At rehearsal he catches the smell of sweat and alcohol in a cramped backstage hallway and suddenly he is back in that room, heart hammering, hands cold on the neck of his instrument. He begins startling when anyone comes up behind him. He chooses seats facing doors, scans green rooms before entering, and finds excuses to avoid venues with narrow corridors or unlit storage areas. On stage he can still perform, often flawlessly, but there are nights when his concentration splinters and he loses his place for a beat because an image flashes across his mind with such force that he feels physically struck by it.

At home he grows quieter. His wife notices first that he does not sleep. He paces downstairs at 3 a.m., checks the locks twice, then a third time. When he does sleep, he wakes drenched in sweat, disoriented and ashamed, with the sensory residue of the assault still vivid in his body. She reaches for him and sometimes he flinches before he can stop himself. He hates that reaction and withdraws further because he cannot explain it without exposing something he feels humiliated by. He has absorbed, against his better judgment, the idea that men are not supposed to be overpowered this way. The shame settles heavily on him. He tells himself he should have fought harder, should have seen it coming, should be able to “get over it.”

His world narrows over time. He turns down out-of-town performances because hotels and unfamiliar venues make him uneasy. He stops staying after shows to talk, packing up quickly and leaving before crowds gather around him. He drinks more than he used to, mostly to bring down the level of tension in his body enough to sleep, though he knows by now it often makes the nights worse. Ordinary touch becomes complicated. Intimacy with his wife is unpredictable; sometimes he wants closeness desperately, and sometimes the shift of weight on a mattress or the sense of being unable to move for even a second sends panic through him. On those nights he makes an excuse—fatigue, a sore back, too much on his mind—and sees the hurt and confusion in her face.

By the present, he lives with the sense that danger can emerge without warning, even in places once associated with pleasure and work. Music remains one of the few areas in which he still feels briefly intact, yet it is no longer uncomplicated. A dark backstage hallway, a hand on his shoulder, laughter from a group of intoxicated men after a set—any of it can cause his body to tense before he has time to think. He says he is exhausted by the effort of managing himself: the avoidance, the vigilance, the constant negotiation between wanting his old life back and fearing the situations that resemble the night it was taken from him. Even with his wife, who has stayed beside him through his silence and fragments of disclosure, he feels at times like a man standing just outside his own life, listening to it as if from behind a closed door.
